analysis.one_liner: Bases Medicare Part D drug coinsurance on the net negotiated price instead of the higher list price.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to lower seniors' Medicare drug coinsurance has sat without any action in two House committees since February 2025, drawing only two cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require Medicare's prescription drug benefit to calculate a senior's coinsurance share of a drug's cost from the plan's actual negotiated price, net of manufacturer discounts, whenever that is lower than the drug's list price (wholesale acquisition cost). Today, coinsurance percentages are applied to the higher list price, so beneficiaries can pay more than the plan actually pays after rebates and discounts. Starting in 2026, seniors in the initial coverage phase would owe coinsurance on the lower, real-world price.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Part D enrollees who face percentage-based coinsurance on their drugs between the annual deductible and the out-of-pocket ceiling. If a plan negotiated a lower net price than the list price, the beneficiary's percentage share would be calculated on the lower number, directly lowering out-of-pocket costs.

how_it_helps.text: Requires that coinsurance for covered Part D drugs be based on the drug's actual acquisition cost — the negotiated plan price net of manufacturer price concessions — whenever that is lower than the wholesale acquisition cost [S2] [S3].
Applies to plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, for costs above the annual deductible and below the annual out-of-pocket threshold, where percentage coinsurance applies [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Part D plan sponsors and the pharmacy benefit intermediaries behind them, who today can charge beneficiaries coinsurance on the higher list price while paying the lower negotiated price and keep the difference. Drug manufacturers are unaffected in what they receive, since the bill redirects existing discounts toward beneficiaries rather than extracting new ones.
analysis.who_pays_short: Part D insurers and pharmacy middlemen

drawbacks.text: The relief is narrow: it applies only to drugs subject to percentage coinsurance rather than flat copays, only in the cost band between the deductible and the out-of-pocket threshold, and excludes drugs described in paragraphs (8) and (9) of the statute [S3].

Plans could respond by converting coinsurance drugs to flat copays, raising premiums, or using other cost-sharing tools to recoup the spread, so the savings for any given senior are not guaranteed [S2].
The calculation depends on plan-reported data (the Detailed DIR Report of prior-year net prices), which may lag and may not reflect current-year negotiations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: it stops plans from charging seniors a percentage of an inflated list price when the true negotiated price is lower. The cost falls on plan intermediaries' margins, and the main risk is that plans restructure cost-sharing to offset it. It is a targeted fix to a pricing mechanism, not a broad drug-price overhaul.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2025 and referred to two House committees, which have taken no action on it since; the Congress is still in session, so it could still move, but so far it has gone nowhere.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald G. Davis (D-NC) introduced the bill on February 12, 2025, joined by Rep. August Pfluger (R-TX) [S1] [S3] [S4].

The same day, it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee, where Medicare-related provisions typically must be approved before reaching the floor [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — appears in the action history [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, Part D plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit intermediaries, who continue to collect coinsurance based on the higher list price while paying lower net prices; seniors' out-of-pocket drug costs remain unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Part D insurers and pharmacy middlemen

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only sponsors are one Democrat (Davis of North Carolina) and one Republican (Pfluger of Texas), and no opposition has been recorded; with just two cosponsors, no meaningful partisan lineup has formed.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: These intermediaries currently charge beneficiaries coinsurance on the drug's higher list price while paying the lower negotiated, rebate-adjusted price, keeping the difference. The bill would channel that spread back to seniors as lower coinsurance.

Manufacturers would pay nothing new — the bill simply redirects concessions they already give plans toward beneficiaries' coinsurance. Their list prices, which anchor the current higher coinsurance, would no longer determine what seniors pay.

analysis.trajectory: A narrowly scoped Medicare billing fix with two cosponsors, idling in two committees for months, rarely reaches the floor on its own. Its most realistic path is absorption into a larger Medicare or health package; absent that, it will likely die at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote.
